Mourners accompany the hearse carrying the remains of CD Tenerife player Jesus de Miguel at his funeral in Navahermosa, central Spain. [Andrea Comas/AP Photo]By APPublished On 5 Nov 20265 Nov 2026
Spain’s national football team coach and the president of Real Madrid joined family, friends and teammates on Thursday at the funeral of Jesus de Miguel, the Tenerife player who died after an on‑field collision earlier this week.
The service was held in Navahermosa, a town of about 3,000 people in central Spain, where De Miguel’s parents were reportedly born.
A hearse covered in flowers moved slowly towards the church as dozens of mourners, some carrying candles, walked behind. The town hall declared three days of mourning, with flags at half-staff.
De Miguel, 30, suffered cardiac arrest after colliding with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono while challenging for a high ball during a second‑division match on Monday. He died in hospital the following day.
Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Real Madrid President Florentino Perez attended the funeral, with De la Fuente saying the game’s community “stands united” in grief.
Police have opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter to assess whether the challenge went beyond normal play.
Tributes have poured in from clubs across Europe, with De Miguel’s death described as a rare and shocking tragedy in professional football.Mourners carry the coffin of De Miguel during his funeral in Navahermosa. People take part in a demonstration in Marseille, France. Trade unions called for a nationwide day of protests against government policy. [Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA]By AP, EPA and ReutersPublished On 5 Nov 20265 Nov 2026
Tens of thousands of trade union members joined nationwide strikes and demonstrations across France on Thursday, demanding higher wages and backing a growing high school protest movement, in a major show of pressure on President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
After more than a month of recurring rallies over the rising cost of living, major marches were held again in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities, with unions saying about 260 protests were planned nationwide.
Students staged new actions, with about a third of France’s high schools closed or unable to operate due to student blockades or teachers walking off the job.
Public transport services were heavily disrupted, and the Eiffel Tower was shut for the day. Police in the northeastern city of Strasbourg urged residents to exercise “extreme caution” near certain schools amid tensions.
In Paris, the atmosphere at Place de la Republique was largely festive despite a heavy security presence, after earlier protests on October 17 were marred by rioting and looting.
Protesters gathered under trade union banners as hundreds of musicians played brass, string and percussion instruments, accompanied by choirs, turning the square into a noisy, colourful focal point of dissent over France’s mounting economic woes.Labour union representatives attend a demonstration in Paris as part of a nationwide day of strikes and protests over wages. Kozo Tashima, honorary president of the Japan Football Association, said on Thursday he will stand against Gianni Infantino in FIFA’s presidential election in March.
Tashima is the second person to declare he will challenge Infantino, following former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega.
The 68-year-old Tashima, who has served on the FIFA Council, said in a statement: “With the full support of the JFA I have decided to declare my candidacy in the FIFA presidential election.
“I believe it is important that the sincerity, integrity and high ethical standards that Japanese football has long valued and built up are clearly communicated to the global football community.
“In order to share these principles with the world and contribute to a better future for football, I have decided to run in the FIFA presidential election.”
Tashima, who was JFA president from 2016 to 2024, added, “Drawing on the experience I have gained over the years, I will take on this challenge with firm resolve so that I can contribute to the further development of world football.”
The deadline for candidates to declare for the election is November 18.
Incumbent Infantino, who is seeking to be re-elected to a fourth and final term as FIFA president, had faced stinging criticism and calls to quit after his aborted World Cup selloff plan.
But Infantino is now in a strong position to secure re-election after the Asian Football Confederation endorsed the 56-year-old last month.
Infantino earlier said he had the backing of the “vast, vast majority” of member associations, and dismissed calls for him to go.

Cristiano Ronaldo has announced his retirement from international football, ending a record-breaking 23-year career with Portugal.
The 41-year-old’s decision, announced on Thursday, brings an end to weeks of speculation about his international career after a public falling-out with Portugal’s head coach, Jorge Jesus.
Ronaldo is one of the most famous footballers of all time and enjoys the highest social media following of all athletes. Over the past few weeks, his millions of worldwide fans have wondered whether the forward’s career had ended on a bitter note.
Here’s a look at the events that unfolded prior to Ronaldo’s announcement:
What sparked the controversy between Ronaldo and Jesus?
On September 30, Ronaldo made an abrupt departure from Portugal’s training camp ahead of the team’s UEFA Nations League fixture against Denmark, prompting a string of questions and a few answers.
Ronaldo confirmed ⁠⁠that he had left after a ⁠⁠turbulent few hours in Copenhagen, amid reports of ⁠⁠a dispute with coach Jesus.
The captain’s decision to walk out came as a shock, as he had been due to train with his teammates at the Parken Stadium.
What happened between Ronaldo and Jesus?
Ronaldo left shortly after the head coach’s news conference, where Jesus confirmed that the five-time Ballon d’Or winner would be left out of his starting lineup for the match against Denmark, marking a second consecutive Nations League game absence.

Iran’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, is exercising power without appearing in public or allowing his voice to be heard. Since succeeding his father in March, he has governed through written statements and decrees, while reports of his meetings with senior officials offer a glimpse into how he exercises power.
The meetings announced in May and August appeared intended primarily to reassure Iranians that their new leader was alive and exercising authority. But a series of four meetings announced within 11 days in October, involving the heads of Iran’s parliament, judiciary and national security establishment, as well as senior military commanders, suggests something more: a new system of decision-making taking shape.
The meetings come as Tehran weighs its options between negotiations and renewed confrontation with the United States and Israel. They also invite comparisons with the consultations that preceded the 2015 nuclear agreement. The question is whether Iran’s new leadership is preparing for a similarly consequential decision, and whether this system is capable of making one.

British comedian and actor Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault by a London court and could face a lengthy prison sentence.
A jury at London’s Southwark Crown Court on Thursday convicted the 51-year-old of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand, who was one of the most prominent broadcasters in Britain and the former husband of American pop star Katy Perry, had denied the allegations. He maintained that the encounters were consensual or that the allegations had been fabricated.
Prosecutors described Brand, who starred in the films Get Him to the Greek and Arthur, as a “ruthless” sexual predator.
Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand would be sentenced on Monday and faced a lengthy prison term. Brand was taken into custody following the verdict.
Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London’s Metropolitan Police said the conviction was “a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them”.
“Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women,” Furphy said.
“As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement.”
